prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) concept for future air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS); one interpretation of Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document. Current NAS: ATM automation predicts trajectories from flight plan plus departure time; controllers issue uncommunicated 'open trajectory' vectors/altitude/speed clearances; Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA); Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) correct; Traffic Flow Management (TFM) reroutes left to controllers. MBT: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users (commercial, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, on-demand) negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs): closed trajectories from current state to destination, for all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft. All constraints affecting an aircraft are reflected in its 4DT; aircraft follow assigned 4DTs complying with trajectory constraints; equipped aircraft substantially responsible. A NAS Constraint Service publishes common NAS constraint information (dynamic e.g. TFM, static e.g. crossing restrictions) to all stakeholders, airspace users and automation. Trajectory constraints map to NAS constraints to identify affected aircraft when NAS constraints change; constraints and tolerances defined per flight performance capability and situational need. Traffic managers apply constraints to amend trajectories as NAS events evolve (fixing route-amendment backlogs). Downstream effects of actions, including tactical control, are considered in trajectory decisions. Time-based performance metric complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN) metrics so a single ATM concept manages all IFR aircraft (avoids mixed-equipage issue of time of arrival control (TOAC) standards). Other improvements: accurate consistent 4DT data shared among users, aircraft and FAA automation; trajectory changes published and synchronized in advance between ground automation and aircraft via air-ground/ground-ground data communications; controllers use strategic closed clearances; demand matches capacity, reducing delay. Actors: FAA, airspace users, pilots, controllers, traffic managers, traffic management automation, ground automation, aircraft automation, NAS Constraint Service, stakeholders.

Document units:
U0051: Traffic management automation will identify which flights are affected by each TMI and translate that TMI into one or more trajectory constraints specific to the flight.  Aircraft provide detailed information about their predicted 4DT (a.k.a. intent data) that is shared across stakeholders.
U0052: Aircraft provide updates when intent data change.  Conflicts can be detected further in advance due to improved predictability, and intervention can be accomplished through adding or modifying constraints in the assigned 4DT.  Open trajectories (i.e., tactical vectoring by controllers) for which the controller’s and/or pilot’s intent is unknown by other actors in the system are minimized.  MBT follows two paths to eliminating open trajectories: 1) introducing methods for planning tactical maneuvers as closed trajectory modifications and 2) eliminating the need for tactical maneuvers through improved predictability.  Digital air-ground communication is used to deliver 4DTs to aircraft cockpits for easy loading and execution in the Flight Management System (FMS).  Broadband air-ground communications and advanced electronic flight bag (EFB) applications are used to include the flight crew in the trajectory negotiation process.  A negotiating controller subsumes the responsibilities of the D-side controller.
U0053: Together, the negotiating controller and traffic management coordinators (TMCs), with their longer time horizon perspectives, proactively intervene to avoid conflicts and achieve TFM objectives, using automation enhancements that facilitate coordinating 4DT changes across multiple sectors. 1.3 Purpose This document is intended to describe a far-term MBT concept.
U0054: Far-term is not precisely defined but targets an operational environment in which the NAS, and the vast majority of aircraft, are capable of the advanced data exchange and automation capabilities associated with the Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2).
U0055: The value of this document is to provide a vector to guide research. 1.4 Near- vs.
U0056: Far-Term MBT This MBT Concept of Operations (ConOps) presents an end-state vision for MBT, while beginning to identify what could be feasible in the more near-term timeframe.
U0057: The near- and far- term MBT concepts differ in two ways.
